title: Multiplication starts with equal groups
description: A few bowls of fruit can explain multiplication. Build equal groups, count them, and explore a times table without memorising it first.

cover.alt: Three bowls with two clementines in each bowl
cover.credit: AI-generated photorealistic image created for BrainiLab.

practice: Ready for a faster challenge? Math Rush is optional; come back to these counters whenever you need them.

sections.title: Three bowls, two pieces of fruit in each
sections.html:
Imagine 3 bowls. Put 2 clementines in every bowl. Each bowl has the same amount: that is what “equal groups” means.

  1. The first bowl gives you two clementines.
  2. The second bowl adds two more. You now have four.
  3. The third bowl adds another two. You now have six.

You could write this as 2 + 2 + 2 = 6. Multiplication gives us a shorter way to describe those equal groups.

sections.title: Build your own groups
sections.html:
Choose a number of groups and how many counters belong in each. Each outline is one group. Before showing the total, count the counters or add one group at a time.

Try 3 groups of 2 first. Then keep 3 groups but put 4 in each. More counters in every group means more counters altogether.

The table below lets you explore bigger examples too. Choose a cell to highlight its row and column. You do not need to learn the whole table today.

sections.title: A shorter way to write equal groups
sections.html:
The sign × means “times”. In this lesson, 3 × 2 means “three groups of two”. We counted six clementines, so 3 × 2 = 6.

The answer to a multiplication is called the product. Here, the product is six. You may see an asterisk, *, used for multiplication on a computer.

The arrangement changes, but the total stays six. You can check this by moving six real counters into those groups.

sections.title: The groups must really be equal
sections.html:
Suppose one bowl has 2 clementines and another has 3. That is not two groups of two. The bowls hold different amounts.

Add the actual amounts instead: two and three make five. The equal-groups shortcut only fits when every group has the same size.

What about three empty bowls? Each holds zero clementines. Altogether there are still none: 3 × 0 = 0.

sections.title: Try four pairs
sections.html:
There are four pairs of socks. A pair means two socks. How many socks are there?

Show me the steps

Count two socks for each pair: 2, then 4, then 6, then 8. Four groups of two make 8 socks.

You have now met adding, taking away and equal groups. Take your time with the short round below. You can return to any activity whenever you like.

For a later challenge, try counting ten groups and one more. For now, understanding the small groups is enough.

questions.prompt: Three bowls each hold 2 clementines. How many clementines are there?
questions.explanation: Count two in the first bowl, two more to make four, and two more to make six.

questions.prompt: Which story matches 4 × 2 in this lesson?
questions.explanation: Each pair holds two socks. Four equal pairs contain eight socks.

questions.prompt: Three bowls each hold 0 clementines. How many clementines are there?
questions.explanation: All three bowls are empty. Empty groups still contain no clementines.
